title: Prevent migraine attacks through targeted CGRP-pathway treatment

concept.text: Reduce migraine frequency with medicines developed against a validated migraine pathway. Erenumab established the approved preventive antibody class; treatment reduces attacks rather than constituting a permanent cure. Proposed completion test: FDA approval for adult migraine prevention, supported by randomized trials showing superiority to placebo in monthly migraine days over 3–6 months and in the proportion achieving at least a 50% reduction. Test set by: FDA; the pivotal protocols prespecified monthly migraine days and 50%-responder endpoints. Reported achieved: FDA approved erenumab (Aimovig) on 17 May 2018. Sources given: [FDA Aimovig approval letter](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2018/761077Orig1s000Approv.pdf) ; [Aimovig prescribing information and trial outcomes](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=b998ed05-94b0-47fd-b28f-cddd1e128fd8&type=display).

page.title: CGRP-targeted migraine prevention
page.definition: Medicines that block calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a nerve-signalling peptide, or its receptor reduce migraine frequency in adults when given preventively. Prevention means fewer migraine days during treatment.

goal.need: The American Headache Society stated in 2024 that preventive therapy is indicated in approximately 40% of people with migraine, although only a minority use it. It attributed part of this gap to limitations in the efficacy and tolerability of established preventive medicines.

statements.quote: The CGRP-targeting therapies should be considered as a first-line approach for migraine prevention

statements.body: US Food and Drug Administration, Eric Bastings, deputy director of the Division of Neurology Products
statements.quote: We need new treatments for this painful and often debilitating condition.
statements.context: The statement accompanied FDA approval of erenumab for adult migraine prevention.

completion.title: The FDA approves a CGRP-pathway medicine for preventive treatment of migraine in adults.
completion.criterion: A medicine that blocks CGRP or its receptor receives FDA marketing approval with an indication for the preventive treatment of migraine in adults.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Aimovig biologics licence application 761077 approval letter.
completion.threshold_quote: We have approved your BLA for Aimovig (erenumab-aooe) effective this date.
completion.basis: Achieved on 17 May 2018 with erenumab (Aimovig). The approved indication encompasses episodic and chronic migraine. The supporting programme included two episodic-migraine trials and one chronic-migraine trial. A reduction of at least 50% in monthly migraine days was a secondary trial endpoint.

milestones.title: Preclinical evidence permits human testing of a CGRP-pathway medicine.
milestones.criterion: Supply pharmacology and toxicology evidence supporting the conclusion that proposed human investigations are reasonably safe, under 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8). Erenumab inhibited human-receptor signalling in cell assays, with half-maximal inhibition at 2.3 nM, and inhibited capsaicin-induced skin blood-flow increases in cynomolgus monkeys (6 per group; intravenous doses 0.1–30 mg/kg). FDA allowed IND 116098 to proceed on 16 October 2012. These enabling results apply to both migraine cases.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8); the preclinical requirement applies before human investigation.
milestones.threshold_quote: the sponsor has concluded that it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations.

milestones.title: A CGRP-pathway medicine reaches initial human dosing in a phase 1 study.
milestones.criterion: Perform initial human dosing with closely monitored pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic and safety assessments. Erenumab's single-dose study treated 60 adults (48 healthy, 12 with migraine; 42 erenumab, 18 placebo): 1–210 mg subcutaneously or 140 mg intravenously. The phase 1 report, first published 24 July 2017, found >75% inhibition of capsaicin-induced skin blood flow after single doses. These human pharmacology results precede separate efficacy tests in the two migraine cases.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, phase 1 definition in 21 CFR 312.21(a); this human-dosing stage is shared by both migraine cases.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: A CGRP-pathway medicine reduces monthly migraine days versus placebo in a phase 2 trial.
milestones.criterion: Meet the protocol's primary superiority test for monthly migraine days during weeks 9–12. Erenumab results: episodic migraine, 483 randomized, 70 mg monthly, reductions 3.4 versus 2.3 days (p=0.021; two-sided α=0.05 with sequential dose testing; published 12 February 2016); chronic migraine, 667 randomized, 70/140 mg monthly, reductions 6.6/6.6 versus 4.2 days (both p<0.0001; initial α=0.04/0.01 with hierarchical testing; published 28 April 2017). Both trials used 12 weeks of blinded subcutaneous treatment.
milestones.set_by: Amgen, protocols NCT01952574 for episodic migraine and NCT02066415 for chronic migraine, described in their primary publications. The quoted endpoint is from the episodic-migraine protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: the change in monthly migraine days from baseline to the last 4 weeks of the 12-week double-blind treatment phase.

milestones.title: A CGRP-pathway medicine meets its phase 3 superiority test for migraine prevention.
milestones.criterion: Meet prespecified phase 3 superiority tests against placebo. Episodic migraine: STRIVE, 955 randomized, erenumab 70/140 mg monthly; mean monthly migraine days over months 4–6, α=0.04/0.01; reductions 3.2/3.7 versus 1.8 days. Chronic migraine: HALO, 1,130 randomized, fremanezumab 675 mg once or 675 mg then 225 mg at weeks 4 and 8; mean monthly qualifying headache days over 12 weeks, two-sided α=0.05; reductions 4.3/4.6 versus 2.5 days. Qualifying days require ≥4 consecutive hours of pain with ≥moderate peak severity or triptan/ergot use for headache. Both reports: 30 November 2017; all four comparisons p<0.001.
milestones.set_by: Amgen and Novartis, STRIVE protocol NCT02456740 for episodic migraine; Teva Pharmaceuticals, HALO protocol NCT02621931 for chronic migraine. The quoted significance thresholds apply to STRIVE.
milestones.threshold_quote: at an alpha level of 0.04 for 70 mg and of 0.01 for 140 mg.

results.finding: Erenumab IND 116098 (sample size not applicable) was allowed to proceed on 16 October 2012.
results.detail: The FDA review also reports human-receptor inhibition at 2.3 nM, a monkey pharmacodynamics study with six animals per group, and supporting safety and toxicology studies.
results.quote:
The IND was submitted September 18, 2012, and allowed to proceed on October 16, 
2012.

results.finding: STRIVE: 955 patients randomized; erenumab met the primary superiority test versus placebo at both doses (p<0.001 for each).
results.detail: Over months 4–6, mean monthly migraine days fell by 3.2 and 3.7 with 70 mg and 140 mg erenumab, respectively, versus 1.8 with placebo. Prespecified alpha levels were 0.04 and 0.01.
results.quote:
From baseline to the final 3 months of the 
double-blind treatment phase, the reduction in 
mean migraine days per month was 3.2 days in 
the 70-mg erenumab group and 3.7 days in the 
140-mg erenumab group, as compared with 1.8 
days in the placebo group (P<0.001 for each dose 
vs. placebo)

results.finding: In 1,130 randomized patients with chronic migraine, both fremanezumab regimens beat placebo on the primary endpoint (P<0.001).
results.detail: Over 12 weeks, mean monthly qualifying headache days fell by 4.3 with quarterly fremanezumab and 4.6 with monthly fremanezumab, versus 2.5 with placebo. The prespecified hierarchical testing procedure controlled the two-sided type I error rate at 0.05.
results.quote:
The least-squares mean (±SE) reduction in the average number of headache days 
per month was 4.3±0.3 with fremanezumab quarterly, 4.6±0.3 with fremanezumab 
monthly, and 2.5±0.3 with placebo (P<0.001 for both comparisons with placebo).
